screens.narratorSegment: Core mechanics are the handful of actions players repeat across most play sessions. screens.title: What is a Core Mechanic?
screens.narratorSegment: A core mechanic is the small set of essential actions that players repeat often and that produce the game's primary play experience. Think of these mechanics as verbs: they describe what players do, like jump, shoot, or rotate. The purpose of naming core mechanics is twofold. First, it clarifies what must be built and polished to make the game fun. Second, it creates a shared vocabulary for the team so designers, artists, and programmers align on what matters most. A concrete example is Super Mario Bros., where jump, run, and stomp comprise the playable vocabulary; those verbs directly inform level design, enemy behavior, and player feedback. A common misconception is treating every interesting idea as core. Not every feature needs to be immediately implemented; many are secondary systems that enrich rather than define play. Another misconception is confusing polish with new mechanics: polishing the core often yields more impact than adding a new action. Key takeaway: name the minimal set of verbs that still make the game satisfying when isolated. Try stripping all else away and testing that concentrated interaction. If it feels empty, your listed mechanics may still be incomplete or not inherently fun.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is a Core Mechanic?
Definition

A core mechanic is a focused set of repeated player actions that define moment-to-moment play and the game's immediate goals. These are the verbs players use to interact with the system.

Why it matters
  • Directs design and polish priorities so work focuses on what players do most.
  • Reduces ambiguity for the team by naming the essential interactions.
  • Makes prototypes faster because you prototype verbs, not complete systems.
Example
Super Mario: jump, run, stomp. These verbs alone steer level design and enemy patterns.
Concrete checks
  • Can the mechanic be described as a verb? If not, refine it.
  • Does it repeat frequently during play? If not, it may be secondary.
  • When isolated, does it still produce satisfying decisions? If not, revise.
Key Takeaway

Name a few verbs and test them alone; polish those before adding supporting features.

screens.title: Core vs Secondary Mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: Distinguishing core mechanics from secondary mechanics prevents scope bloat and keeps the player's immediate experience clear. Core mechanics are essential; the game relies on them for its moment-to-moment fun. Secondary mechanics add depth or variety, but they are not required for the game to be playable or recognizable. For example, in a role-playing game, combat and exploration are often core; crafting potions or changing outfits are secondary. One practical test is the isolation test: remove secondary systems and see if the game still captures its intended experience. Another test is frequency: core mechanics are used repeatedly, often every few minutes or less. A common pitfall is treating a novel or flashy idea as core simply because it excites the team. That leads to feature creep and dilutes the design. Keep a short list of core verbs and allow secondary ideas to remain on a backlog until the core is solid. Example: a crafting system is valuable, but if early players never engage with it, it should be postponed. This keeps development focused and prototypes meaningful. Core vs Secondary Mechanics means core mechanics repeat and survive removal of extras; secondary mechanics enrich but are optional early on.. In practical terms, how to distinguish essential actions from supporting features. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Core vs Secondary Mechanics
Comparison grid
Core Mechanics
  • Repeated frequently
  • Essential to loop
  • Polish increases fun
  • Examples: jump, shoot, solve
Secondary Mechanics
  • Enhance or decorate
  • Optional for play
  • Can be deferred to later
  • Examples: crafting, trading, cosmetics
Practical checks
  1. Isolation test: remove the system. Does the core experience survive?
  2. Frequency test: how often will a player use this action during play?
  3. Value test: does this mechanic change the primary decisions players make?
Common mistake
Confusing novelty with necessity leads to feature creep. Reserve flashy ideas for after the core is solid.

screens.title: From Verbs to Loop
screens.narratorSegment: Turning verbs into a loop is a practical design step. Start by listing 3–5 verbs you expect the player to use most. Then ask: what triggers each verb, what feedback follows, and how does the result lead to the next action? The loop is a tiny sequence that repeats: find a target, act, receive feedback, and decide the next target. For a first-person shooter the loop reads: find enemy, aim, shoot, reload, find cover, repeat. For a puzzle game the loop could be: observe puzzle, form hypothesis, test solution, evaluate outcome, repeat. The process helps you see whether verbs chain together logically and whether the chain is satisfying when repeated. A useful practice is to write the loop as four or five short steps and then prototype only those steps. A common misconception is assuming that the loop must always include progression systems; instead, small feedback loops can be inherently satisfying without long-term progression. Key takeaway: keep the loop compact, test it quickly, and iterate until each step feels engaging on its own and as part of the sequence. From Verbs to Loop means a clear loop links triggers, actions, and feedback so players feel rhythm and purpose in repeated play.. In practical terms, turn named verbs into a primary gameplay loop. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › From Verbs to Loop
Step-by-step
  1. List the most frequent verbs (3–5).
  2. For each verb, define triggers and feedback.
  3. Chain verbs into a short repeating sequence.
  4. Prototype these steps and iterate rapidly.
Example loop (FPS)
Find enemy → Aim → Shoot → Reload → Find cover → Repeat
Practice card
Write a 4-step loop for one mechanic from your idea. Keep steps short and test whether repeating those steps produces decisions the player cares about.
Key Takeaway

A loop is not a long feature list; it is a compact cycle that feels satisfying every iteration.

screens.title: Game Verbs: Naming Interactions
screens.narratorSegment: Game verbs are concise action words that describe what players do: jump, scan, collect, dodge, build. Naming verbs forces specificity. Instead of writing 'player can interact with objects', write 'scan object' or 'pick up resource.' This precision matters because verbs are the smallest unit you can prototype and measure. For example, in the robot exploration concept the verbs were Scan, Collect, Move, Avoid. Each verb implies a small interaction pattern: scan targets provide information, collect adds items to inventory, move navigates terrain, avoid triggers danger-based decisions. When you document verbs, include the expected inputs, the feedback the player receives, and the desired emotional response. A mistake is making verbs too broad, like 'interact', which hides several distinct actions and makes prototyping ambiguous. Concrete exercise: pick one verb and list the target, the player input, the immediate feedback, and the follow-up decision it should provoke. That structure gives your team a lightweight specification you can test with a paper or digital prototype. In practical terms, turn actions into precise verbs that guide prototyping. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Game Verbs
Verb template
Verb: Scan
Target: Object with readable data
Input: Activate scanner / press button
Feedback: Data panel, sound, visual highlight
Follow-up: Decide whether to collect or ignore
Example
Robot game verbs: Scan, Collect, Move, Avoid — each leads to distinct choices and can be prototyped individually.
Practice prompt

screens.title: Designing a Simple Core Mechanic
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a simple core mechanic is best done in four steps: define the verb, sketch a minimal interaction, determine feedback, and prototype. First, define the verb in one clear word. Second, sketch the minimal interaction in steps the player takes from trigger to result. Third, specify feedback that communicates success, failure, and skill expression. Fourth, build a quick prototype — paper, clickable slides, or a short script — that isolates this mechanic. For example, the robot exploration game uses Scan: target object, press scan, display discovered data, add a small timer or resource reward. The minimal prototype could be a slide where a user points at an object and clicks to see a result. The goal is not to build a full system but to validate whether the interaction is satisfying and whether it leads to repeatable decisions. A common pitfall is overbuilding the prototype to include secondary mechanics, which obscures whether the core itself works. Keep prototypes narrow and iterate until the mechanic feels good as a loop on its own. Designing a Simple Core Mechanic means prototype one verb with clear feedback and iterate until the isolated interaction is satisfying.. In practical terms, a stepwise approach from idea to paper prototype. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

  2. Sketch the minimal interaction sequence.
  3. Specify clear feedback for success and failure.

  • Log decisions that follow the interaction to see if it leads to meaningful choices.

screens.title: Robot Exploration — A Worked Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the supplied robot exploration example to see every step in practice. Start by naming verbs: Scan, Collect, Move, Avoid. For Scan, the interaction is: target object, activate scanner, read data. Collect requires approach, initiate collection, and receive an item. Move covers navigation choices and risk/reward decisions while Avoid implies quick reactions to hazards. From these verbs we form a loop centered on exploration and survival: move to a new area, scan for resources, decide to collect or bypass, navigate hazards to return to base or continue. Each verb produces feedback that feeds the next decision. When prototyping, isolate one verb at a time. Test Scan as a target-and-reveal interaction, and see whether players want to scan repeatedly. A common misconception is assuming the full system must be present. Instead, validate each verb's core satisfaction, then layer. This staged validation protects your schedule and makes the final integrated system far more stable and coherent. After testing, ask whether the loop still reads as exploration and survival when secondary systems are removed. screens.title: Feature Creep and Scope Control
screens.narratorSegment: Feature creep happens when ideas are continuously added without checking how they affect the core loop. It is especially dangerous early in development because it dilutes focus and increases implementation time. One practical mitigation is to define a strict minimum viable product (MVP) centered on the core mechanics. Ask: what must exist for the loop to be enjoyable? Anything else is secondary until the core proves itself. Use a simple pruning checklist: does this idea increase the frequency of core interactions, deepen decisions within the loop, or merely add variety? If it fails those tests, defer it. Another practical tip is timeboxing features — give a short window to prototype an idea, then evaluate against the MVP. A common misconception is believing that more systems equal deeper gameplay. Unchecked features delay releases and hide whether the core loop works. Focused development exposes problems early and keeps player experience coherent.
Pruning checklist

Feature creep often feels productive. Measure impact on the core loop before committing resources.

screens.title: Assessing Core Mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: Assessing whether you correctly identified core mechanics can be both objective and reflective. Objective checks include multiple-choice or short answer questions, like asking which action is most frequently used in a design scenario. The chapter provides a sample question about a wizard: casting spells is the core action, while crafting or decorating are secondary. Reflection prompts help designers surface assumptions: which mechanic did you assume players would enjoy, and why? One useful assessment is to apply the isolation test: remove everything but the core and run a short playtest. If the core still captures the intended play, you passed. If it feels empty, reconsider your verbs or add a tightly integrated mechanic. fullNarratorScript:
Core mechanics are the handful of actions players repeat across most play sessions. They act like verbs in a language: they say what the player does, how the world responds, and what the immediate goals are. In this chapter you will learn how to spot those verbs, separate them from supporting features, and shape them into a satisfying primary gameplay loop. We'll use examples you already know — jumping in platformers, shooting in shooters, rotating blocks in puzzle games — to make the idea concrete. You'll also practice a short design exercise where you list likely core mechanics, name their verbs, and write a compact loop that shows how the actions chain together. Learning to prune and prioritize is just as important as inventing new mechanics. By the end of this lesson you should be able to answer: if I remove everything but the core, is the game still interesting? That question helps you keep your design focused and playable early.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to name core mechanics and explain how they differ from secondary mechanics, describe how those mechanics form a primary gameplay loop, design a simple core mechanic with clear verbs, and evaluate common pitfalls that derail a focused design. Each objective includes a practical reason why it matters. Naming verbs makes communication clear across your team, and distinguishing core from secondary mechanics helps you prioritize what to prototype. Designing a simple mechanic with explicit verbs makes prototyping faster and exposes failure modes early. Finally, recognizing feature creep and lack of clarity lets you keep scope manageable and protect the player's moment-to-moment experience. These are not abstract skills — they directly influence how long your team spends building, how testable your early prototypes are, and whether players immediately understand what the game asks them to do. We'll practice each objective with short tasks that reinforce rapid iteration and disciplined pruning.

Each objective pairs with a short activity so you practice immediately. For articulating core mechanics, you'll list verbs for a familiar game and justify why each is core. For analyzing the loop, you'll write a four-step loop describing the recurring player rhythm. For designing a mechanic, you'll pick a single mechanic, name its verbs, and create a one-paragraph interaction description suitable for a paper or quick prototype. For evaluating pitfalls, you'll run a pruning checklist against a feature idea and decide whether it belongs in the core, as a secondary system, or as post-launch content. These exercises build a muscle for clarity — you learn to spot redundancy, unclear verbs, and actions that break the loop. Practice makes it faster to answer the crucial test: if I strip away everything but this mechanic, is play still satisfying? That test keeps early builds focused and helps your team avoid wasted effort.

A core mechanic is the small set of essential actions that players repeat often and that produce the game's primary play experience. Think of these mechanics as verbs: they describe what players do, like jump, shoot, or rotate. The purpose of naming core mechanics is twofold. First, it clarifies what must be built and polished to make the game fun. Second, it creates a shared vocabulary for the team so designers, artists, and programmers align on what matters most. A concrete example is Super Mario Bros., where jump, run, and stomp comprise the playable vocabulary; those verbs directly inform level design, enemy behavior, and player feedback. A common misconception is treating every interesting idea as core. Not every feature needs to be immediately implemented; many are secondary systems that enrich rather than define play. Another misconception is confusing polish with new mechanics: polishing the core often yields more impact than adding a new action. Key takeaway: name the minimal set of verbs that still make the game satisfying when isolated. Try stripping all else away and testing that concentrated interaction. If it feels empty, your listed mechanics may still be incomplete or not inherently fun.

Distinguishing core mechanics from secondary mechanics prevents scope bloat and keeps the player's immediate experience clear. Core mechanics are essential; the game relies on them for its moment-to-moment fun. Secondary mechanics add depth or variety, but they are not required for the game to be playable or recognizable. For example, in a role-playing game, combat and exploration are often core; crafting potions or changing outfits are secondary. One practical test is the isolation test: remove secondary systems and see if the game still captures its intended experience. Another test is frequency: core mechanics are used repeatedly, often every few minutes or less. A common pitfall is treating a novel or flashy idea as core simply because it excites the team. That leads to feature creep and dilutes the design. Keep a short list of core verbs and allow secondary ideas to remain on a backlog until the core is solid. Example: a crafting system is valuable, but if early players never engage with it, it should be postponed. This keeps development focused and prototypes meaningful. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Turning verbs into a loop is a practical design step. Start by listing 3–5 verbs you expect the player to use most. Then ask: what triggers each verb, what feedback follows, and how does the result lead to the next action? The loop is a tiny sequence that repeats: find a target, act, receive feedback, and decide the next target. For a first-person shooter the loop reads: find enemy, aim, shoot, reload, find cover, repeat. For a puzzle game the loop could be: observe puzzle, form hypothesis, test solution, evaluate outcome, repeat. The process helps you see whether verbs chain together logically and whether the chain is satisfying when repeated. A useful practice is to write the loop as four or five short steps and then prototype only those steps. A common misconception is assuming that the loop must always include progression systems; instead, small feedback loops can be inherently satisfying without long-term progression. Key takeaway: keep the loop compact, test it quickly, and iterate until each step feels engaging on its own and as part of the sequence. Game verbs are concise action words that describe what players do: jump, scan, collect, dodge, build. Naming verbs forces specificity. Instead of writing 'player can interact with objects', write 'scan object' or 'pick up resource.' This precision matters because verbs are the smallest unit you can prototype and measure. For example, in the robot exploration concept the verbs were Scan, Collect, Move, Avoid. Each verb implies a small interaction pattern: scan targets provide information, collect adds items to inventory, move navigates terrain, avoid triggers danger-based decisions. When you document verbs, include the expected inputs, the feedback the player receives, and the desired emotional response. A mistake is making verbs too broad, like 'interact', which hides several distinct actions and makes prototyping ambiguous. Concrete exercise: pick one verb and list the target, the player input, the immediate feedback, and the follow-up decision it should provoke. That structure gives your team a lightweight specification you can test with a paper or digital prototype. Second, sketch the minimal interaction in steps the player takes from trigger to result. Third, specify feedback that communicates success, failure, and skill expression. Fourth, build a quick prototype — paper, clickable slides, or a short script — that isolates this mechanic. For example, the robot exploration game uses Scan: target object, press scan, display discovered data, add a small timer or resource reward.
